procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 27.04.2023 of the High Court at Calcutta in WPA (P) Nos.151, 154, 156 and 162 of 2023.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court's order was supported by the Solicitor General of India appearing on behalf of the NIA and the counsel appearing on behalf of the original petitioners and the intervenors. Two grounds weighed with the High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Petitioners approached the Supreme Court by filing Special Leave Petitions (Criminal) Nos. 6283-6286 of 2023. The Supreme Court was not inclined to entertain the Special Leave Petitions and disposed of them.

issue.issue_text: Whether the exercise of jurisdiction by the Central Government under Section 6(5) of the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008, was extraneous to the powers conferred upon it, warranting the interference of the Court.

facts: Six FIRs were registered between March 30, 2023, and April 3, 2023, concerning various incidents.
Acting on a Public Interest Litigation, the High Court of Calcutta ordered the investigation to be transferred to the National Investigation Agency (NIA).
The High Court directed the Central Government to exercise its power under Section 6(5) of the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008.
Following the High Court's order, the Central Government issued a notification on May 8, 2023, exercising its power under Section 6(5).
Subsequently, the NIA registered six FIRs on May 10, 2023, and a Special Court took cognizance of the matter on May 11, 2023.
law: Section 6(5) of the NIA Act grants the Central Government a 'suo moto' power to direct the NIA to investigate a scheduled offence if it believes it is required.
This power is prefaced by a non-obstante provision, meaning it can be exercised independently of other subsections.
When the Central Government exercises this power, the State Government and its police must cease their investigation and transfer all relevant records to the NIA.
The Central Government must determine if the offence is a 'scheduled offence' and if, considering its gravity and other factors, it is a 'fit case' for NIA investigation.
The Central Government's decision can be based on information from the State Government or from 'other sources'.
application: The Court established that its role was not to assess the sufficiency or veracity of the allegations, but only to determine if the Central Government's action was extraneous to the powers granted by Section 6(5).
The Court noted that the Central Government's notification, while referencing the High Court's order, expressly stated that the power was being exercised under Section 6(5) of the Act.
This sequence of events, which was undisputed, demonstrated that the NIA had exercised its jurisdiction specifically with reference to its statutory powers.
Since the NIA had registered the cases and a Special Court had already taken cognizance, the legal process was properly underway.
The Court concluded that it could not anticipate or restrict the scope of the NIA's investigation at this preliminary stage.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the exercise of jurisdiction by the Central Government under Section 6(5) of the NIA Act was not extraneous to the powers conferred upon it and did not warrant the Court's interference. Therefore, the Court affirmed the judgment of the High Court and rejected the challenge.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the exercise of jurisdiction by the Central Government under Section 6(5) of the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008, was extraneous to the powers conferred upon it, warranting the interference of the Court.
appellant_arguments: The injuries sustained by the complainant were only abrasions, which are inconsistent with the severity of the incident alleged.
The investigation was already being conducted by seven different police officers, including the preparation of seizure memos, indicating a sufficient local response.
respondent_arguments: The respondents (the NIA, the original petitioners before the High Court, and intervenors) supported the High Court's order which upheld the Central Government's exercise of jurisdiction.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where the validity of a notification issued under Section 6(5) of the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008, which confers jurisdiction upon the National Investigation Agency (NIA), is not challenged, the court will not entertain a petition against the transfer of the investigation to the NIA.
obiter: Observations made by a High Court in an order concerning the transfer of an investigation should be confined to the specific question of the validity of the investigating agency's jurisdiction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court's role at this stage is not to evaluate the sufficiency or veracity of the allegations. The only question is whether the Central Government's exercise of jurisdiction under Section 6(5) of the NIA Act was extraneous to its powers. Since the validity of the notification itself was not challenged, and the NIA Court has already taken cognizance, there is no basis for the Supreme Court to interfere with the High Court's decision to uphold the NIA investigation.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the exercise of jurisdiction by the Central Government under Section 6(5) is extraneous to the powers conferred upon it by Section 6(5) so as to warrant the interference of this Court.
why_appellant_lost: The Court is not called upon to decide on the sufficiency of the allegations or their veracity at this stage, rendering the appellant's arguments about the nature of injuries or the adequacy of the local police response irrelevant to the jurisdictional question.
The petitioners did not challenge the validity of the notification which was issued under Section 6(5), which is the legal basis for the NIA's jurisdiction.

The Court determined that the precise contours of an investigation cannot be anticipated or restricted at this stage, especially after a specialized court (the NIA Court) has already taken cognizance of the matter.
why_respondent_won: The Court's review was confined to the narrow question of whether the Central Government's action was extraneous to its statutory powers, a standard the appellant failed to meet.
The legal foundation for the NIA's involvement, the notification under Section 6(5), remained unchallenged.
The investigation had already progressed to the stage where the NIA Court had taken cognizance, making judicial interference in the investigation's scope inappropriate.
policy_considerations: The Court exercises judicial restraint by refusing to interfere with the early stages of an investigation or to anticipate and restrict its scope.
The Court defers to the specialized jurisdiction of the NIA Court once it has taken cognizance of a case.
